title: DfE Decoded #162: The DfE’s new case-study research on school belonging
author: Paul Urry
source: paulurry68.substack.com (DfE Decoded, A Headteacher's Perspective), October 18, 2026
summary: Paul Urry reads the Department for Education's new case-study research on school belonging and argues that what it describes is culture, not a programme. Looking at schools where pupils report strong belonging alongside strong attendance and attainment, the research finds five recurring dimensions: safety and security, inclusion, collective identity, individual recognition and positive relationships. Urry stresses that belonging is not a lowering of expectations, since staff and pupils described high expectations as an act of care, and that belonging, attendance and attainment reinforce each other in a cycle. He emphasises ordinary daily relationships over pastoral structures, pupil voice that visibly changes something, enrichment as a route to status beyond academics, and individualised routes for pupils with SEND. His most pointed finding is that staff belonging comes first, because adults cannot create for pupils what they do not experience themselves. He advises leaders to start with questions about the pupils who find school hardest rather than a belonging action plan.
points: The five dimensions of safety, inclusion, collective identity, individual recognition and positive relationships work as a practical test of any school's culture.
High expectations were described as an act of care, so belonging and standards are allies rather than competitors.
Belonging should sit inside attendance strategy, because absence and disconnection feed each other in a cycle.
Pupil voice only counts if pupils can point to something that changed because adults listened.
Staff belonging comes before pupil belonging, so leaders have to create for their teams what they hope teachers will create for children.
quotes: The answer is not one programme. Not one intervention. Not one policy. It is culture.
Leaders, staff and pupils described high expectations as an act of care.
We know you. You matter here. And because you matter, we expect you to succeed.
Belonging is not the opposite of standards. Done well, it may help make those standards possible.
A pupil who feels unseen by the adults they encounter all day is unlikely to develop a strong sense of belonging because they see a mentor for twenty minutes on Thursday afternoon.
Can pupils point to something in school that is different because adults listened to them? If they can, pupil voice is probably real. If they cannot, we may only be collecting opinions.
Staff cannot consistently create belonging for pupils if they do not experience it themselves.
Children decide whether they belong from hundreds of small experiences.
